newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila orders killing of 645 Ebola-hit monkeys.
newsitem.headline: Manila orders killing of 645 Ebola-hit monkeys.

text.p: The Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) on Friday ordered the killing of 645 monkeys believed infected with the Ebola virus.
"The infected monkeys will first be put to sleep and then disposed of through lethal injection on Saturday. The carcasses will be incinerated," said environment undersecretary Antonio La Vina.
A joint team of the DENR and the Department of Health would kill the Ferlite Scientific Research Inc monkeys in order to prevent the virus from spreading, he said.

"A study group formed by the DENR to investigate the outbreak of the Ebola Reston virus at the Ferlite monkey farm showed that the infection continued to circulate in the facility and has spread beyond the cages where the virus was originally detected," La Vina said.
Ferlite was investigated after two monkeys it exported to the United States in March 1996 were found to have been affected by the Ebola Reston virus, he added.
The firm used to export 1,500 primates a year for experiments in laboratories, officials said.
Environment Secretary Victor Ramos said in a separate statement that even if the possibility that the virus would infect human beings was remote, the government could not take the risk.
La Vina said Ferlite's breeding farm was closed by the DENR on Friday after its farm and collector's permit was cancelled.
Ferlite president Alex Lina said his firm would comply with the closure order of the DENR.
"Although I am still appealing not to kill the animals, I cannot do anything about it," Lina told reporters. He said the 645 monkeys were all those left at the breeding farm.
"They said (the facility) was a health hazard. No one has died, no monkey has died here," Lina said.

The Ebola virus is named after a river in northern Zaire where it was first identified in 1976. The virus causes internal bleeding and an agonising death. Outbreaks in Africa have killed several hundred people.

The Reston strain was named after a 1989 outbreak that wiped out a whole colony of monkeys in a breeding facility in Reston, Virginia. The strain has not been found to cause illness in humans, according to U.S. and Philippine health officials.
